idiom_name: statements before super(): compute the payload into a local or holder, then super(payload)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has the ordering trap and a sanctioned way out that replaces the classic structure. Per the documented class evaluation: for a derived class the constructor body before the super() call is evaluated first (that part 'should not access this because it is not yet initialized'), then super() runs, then the class's own fields are initialized, and only then the rest of the constructor body. So the payload is computed before the call - into a local, or into a holder object when the base must keep a live reference - and handed to super(payload); the object's own data is assigned from the same local afterwards. No helper base is needed and none is possible (single inheritance, and no base-specifier list to order), so the local-before-super idiom is the direct replacement.
pitfalls: Touching this before super() throws, and reading a derived field while the base constructor runs yields undefined (public fields) or a TypeError (private fields), because class fields are initialized only after super() returns - the base sees its own value, not the derived one.

A local cannot give the base the identity of the derived object's own storage: when the base stores a pointer/reference into the object, pass a holder object both sides share (const holder = {}; super(holder)) or restructure the hierarchy.

Assigning this.buf = buf after super() shares the reference rather than copying the value: later mutation is visible on both sides, which is usually intended here but surprising if a snapshot was meant.
